prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Other weddings are so shrewd on the sofa, short and baffled, bassett-legged. All things knuckled, I have no winter left, in my sore rememory, to melt down for drinking water. Shrunk down. Your wedding slides the way wiry dark hairs do, down a swimming pool drain. So I am drained. Sincerely. I wish you every chapped bird on this pilgrimage to hold your hem up from the dust. Dust is plural: infinite dust. I will sink in the sun, I will crawl towards the heavy drawing and design the curtains in the room of never marrying you. Because it is a sinking, because today’s perfect weather is a later life’s smut. This soiled future unplans love. I keep unplanning the same Sunday. Leg and flower, breeze and terrier, I have no garden and couldn’t be happier. Please, don’t lose me here. I am sorry my clutch is all tendon and no discipline: the heart is a severed kind of muscle and alone. I can hear yours in your room. I hear mine in another room. In another’s.

outputs.L1:
Here is a gently polished version that preserves the surreal, lyrical spirit of the original while refining its cadence and flow:

---

Other weddings sit so shrewd upon the sofa—short and baffled, bassett-legged. All things have knuckled under, and I have no winter left in my sore remembrance to melt down for drinking water. Shrunk down. Your wedding slips away the way wiry dark hairs do, sliding down a swimming pool drain. And so I am drained. Sincerely. I wish you every chapped bird on this pilgrimage, each one to hold your hem up from the dust. Dust is plural: infinite dust. I will sink into the sun; I will crawl toward the heavy drawing and design the curtains for the room of never marrying you. Because it is a sinking. Because today's perfect weather is a later life's smut. This soiled future unplans love. I keep unplanning the same Sunday. Leg and flower, breeze and terrier—I have no garden, and I couldn't be happier. Please, don't lose me here. I am sorry my grasp is all tendon and no discipline: the heart is a severed kind of muscle, and alone. I can hear yours in your room. I hear mine in another. In another's.

---

A note: this passage reads as deliberate, avant-garde poetry, where much of its power lies in its strangeness, fractured syntax, and unexpected imagery. I've kept my edits light—smoothing transitions and clarifying a few phrasings—so as not to flatten its distinctive voice. If you'd prefer a more conventionally "professional" rewrite, I'm happy to take the language further in that direction, though it would necessarily alter the poetic effect.
outputs.L2: Different marriages sit so cunningly upon the couch, stubby and confused, their legs bowed like a basset hound's. Everything has turned to bone, and no winter remains within my aching store of memory to thaw into something I could drink. It has all withered away. Your marriage slips down like thin dark strands of hair vanishing into a pool's drain. And so I am emptied out. Truly. I hope every cracked and weathered bird along this journey lifts the edge of your gown clear of the ground. The ground is made of countless specks: endless particles. I will descend into the sunlight, I will drag myself toward the weighty sketch and fashion the drapes for the chamber where I never wed you. For this is a descent, for the flawless skies of today become the grime of some future season. This tainted tomorrow undoes love's blueprint. Again and again I dismantle the plans for that identical Sunday. Limb and blossom, gust of wind and small dog—I possess no garden, yet nothing could bring me greater joy. I beg you, do not misplace me in this spot. Forgive me that my grasp is nothing but sinew without restraint: the heart is a muscle cut loose and solitary. I can catch the sound of yours within your chamber. I catch the sound of mine in some other chamber. Within somebody else's.
outputs.L3:
# On Witnessing Another's Wedding

There is a particular kind of exhaustion that comes from watching happiness that was never meant to be yours. The speaker stands at the edge of someone else's wedding, emotionally drained, mourning a love that was either lost to circumstance or impossible from the beginning. The celebration unfolding before them is not a source of joy but a reminder of everything that will remain forever out of reach.

In the quiet theater of the mind, the speaker constructs an entire parallel existence. They imagine themselves patiently decorating "the room of never marrying you"—a space devoted to a union that will never occur. This is grief turned domestic, the strange labor of tending to a life that exists only in longing. The relationship becomes real precisely through its impossibility, dwelt upon and furnished with all the care one might give to an actual home.

Even the beauty of the present moment offers no comfort. The "perfect weather" of today is not experienced as a gift but transformed into the raw material of future regret. The speaker performs the same painful ritual again and again, "unplanning" a day that was never planned to begin with—repeatedly dismantling an imagined future, only to build and dismantle it once more.

What emerges is a profound paradox. The speaker admits to having "no garden," no cultivated life shared with the beloved, no fruit of a partnership that never took root. And yet, in the same breath, they insist they "couldn't be happier." This contradiction captures the strange equilibrium of acceptance—a contentment that coexists with absence, a peace made from loss rather than fulfillment.

The poem closes on an image of stark and irreversible isolation. The heart is rendered not as a whole but as a "severed" muscle, cut in two, each half beating alone in separate rooms. It is the perfect final metaphor: two people, two chambers, two lives continuing their rhythm in permanent separation—together in their division, yet forever apart.
outputs.L4:
# Heartbreak and Isolation: An Analysis

This poem explores heartbreak and unrequited love through fragmented, surreal imagery, using the occasion of another person's wedding to convey the speaker's sense of loss and emotional depletion. Rather than presenting grief in a linear or straightforward manner, the poem fractures the speaker's experience into disjointed pieces, mirroring the way that emotional devastation can shatter one's sense of coherence and continuity. The surreal quality of the imagery suggests a mind struggling to process an unbearable reality—the world becomes distorted, dreamlike, and disorienting when filtered through the lens of profound loss.

The choice to set this emotional reckoning against the backdrop of a wedding proves particularly effective. A wedding, traditionally a celebration of union and love fulfilled, becomes for the speaker a cruel mirror reflecting everything they cannot have. While others gather to witness a joyful joining of lives, the speaker experiences the opposite: a severing, an ending, a hollowing out. This juxtaposition heightens the emotional stakes, transforming a communal moment of happiness into a private ceremony of mourning. The occasion forces the speaker to confront the finality of their situation—the beloved is not merely unavailable but is actively pledging themselves to another.

The work's power lies in its portrayal of isolation and severed connection—culminating in the image of hearts beating alone in separate rooms—which captures the profound loneliness of loving someone who marries another. This central image resonates with quiet devastation. Two hearts, which might have beaten in harmony, instead pulse in solitude, divided by walls both literal and metaphorical. The image speaks to the fundamental tragedy of unrequited love: the physical proximity that emphasizes emotional distance, the shared humanity that only underscores the impossibility of connection. Each heart continues its steady rhythm, alive and functioning, yet utterly alone—a poignant reminder that survival and healing are not the same thing.

Ultimately, the poem achieves its emotional depth not through dramatic declaration but through this careful accumulation of fragmented images and its haunting final metaphor. It gives voice to a universal yet deeply personal experience: the ache of watching someone you love build a life with another, and the isolating recognition that love, however powerful, cannot always bridge the distance between two separate rooms.
outputs.L5:
# When Everything Feels Smaller

There is a peculiar sensation that comes over us in certain seasons of life, when the world we once knew seems to have **shrunk** around us. The wide-open horizons of childhood, the endless summers, the streets that felt like continents—somehow, all of it has become smaller, more manageable, and sometimes disappointingly so.

## The Illusion of Shrinking

Of course, nothing has physically changed. The house we grew up in remains the same size; it is we who have grown. **All** the rooms that once towered over us now sit comfortably within our grasp. What we perceive as shrinkage is really a matter of perspective—our understanding has expanded, and in doing so, it has made the familiar feel compact.

This is true not only of physical spaces but of challenges as well. A problem that once seemed insurmountable eventually looks trivial once we have gained the experience to face it. In this sense, growth is measured by how much smaller our old fears become.

## Room for the Other

Yet there is a hidden gift in this shrinking. When our own world becomes smaller and more familiar, we create space to notice the **other**—other people, other ideas, other ways of living that we never had the capacity to see before. The mind that once filled every corner with its own concerns can finally welcome perspectives beyond itself.

To recognize the other is to admit that we are not the center of everything. It is a humbling and liberating realization, one that transforms a shrinking world into an expanding community.

## Conclusion

So when it feels as though everything has **shrunk**, remember that **all** perception is relative, and that the smallness you sense may simply be room being made for something—or someone—**other** than yourself. What looks like loss is often the quiet beginning of a larger connection.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal, fragmented prose poem addressed to a lover on their wedding day to someone else, full of grief, unusual imagery, and wordplay.
counterfactuals.output:
# Epithalamium for the Wrong Altar

*

Today you are folded into someone else's laundry, pressed and permanent. I read the announcement in the color of the sky, which is the color of an old bruise learning to forgive its own violence.

*

The word *aisle* is a small island. The word *isle* is where I have been marooned. Listen: even the dictionary keeps us adjacent and drowning.

*

You wore white. I wore the weather. Somewhere a cake divided itself into futures I was not invited to eat.

*

I have been practicing your name until it became a bird, then a broken clock, then a bird again with the hours still ticking in its throat. *Til death*, they said, and I thought: yes, I have already begun.

*

Here is a confession shaped like a fruit: I loved you in the subjunctive. *If I were. Had I only. Would that.* All the tenses that never happen, all the grammar of the almost.

*

The rings you exchanged are two zeros. Two mouths saying *oh.* Two nothings holding hands. Forgive me — grief makes a mathematician of the abandoned, always counting what will not add.

*

Once you told me love was a house. I did not know you meant *for someone else.* I have been standing in the doorway so long the doorway has grown into me. I am the hinge that opens onto no one.

*

Petals. Petals. The flower girl scatters the alphabet of my undoing. *P* for *please.* *P* for the past. *P* for the person I was before I learned that vows are just weather that agrees to stay.

*

And you — luminous, laughing, someone's now — you turn and for one glass second I think you see me in the back row wearing the suit of my own dissolving.

You don't.

The music swells like water in the lungs.

*

I wish you happiness. I mean it the way a wound means the knife: completely, and against my will.

*

Go. Be held. Be the held thing.

I will stay here in the church of the almost, lighting candles that spell nothing, drinking the small dark wine of *what I would have said*

had you asked

had you turned

had the island been an aisle

and the aisle a way back

to me.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose an experimental piece of writing in the style of a heartbroken speaker who is not the one being married, using strange associative language, images of dust, sinking, and severed hearts.
counterfactuals.output:
**THE WEDDING I AM NOT IN**

The invitation came on paper made of skin I used to know.

*RSVP by the dust.* And I have. I have replied with the whole of my sinking, with the slow furniture of my chest going down through the floorboards, down through the sub-floor, down into the part of the house where the pipes forget their names.

You are marrying someone who is not me and the ceremony smells like a jar left open in July.

Listen—

I have taken my heart out to look at it, the way you take a fish from a bag of water, holding it by the tail of what it used to want. Severed. Clean at the root, like a tooth that agreed to leave. I keep it on the windowsill now beside the aspirin and the salt, and it does not beat so much as *powder*. Every morning a little more of it comes off on my thumb.

You are wearing white, they tell me. Of course. White is the color of what falls off things. White is dust before it settles. White is the inside of the envelope where my name went unwritten, where instead there was a *plus one*, that stranger, that placeholder, that country I was exiled into and then removed from.

I am sinking through the guest list.

Somewhere a cake is being cut and I feel it in the meridian that runs from my sternum to the last time you said my name like it wasn't heavy.

The bees have moved into the severed part. Did I mention. In the chamber where you used to be there is now a low industrious humming and a smell of something sweet and abandoned, and I do not know how to evict them, and I do not want to, because at least the humming is *company*, at least the humming has the decency to stay.

Confetti. Or is it me. Some of me has become the small torn things that fall on people who are happy. I am in the air above the aisle. I am the tiny paper hearts, all of them severed, all of them shaped like the wound and thrown for luck.

Congratulations. I say it and my mouth fills with grout.

The dust is rising now to meet the sinking, halfway down the house we are shaking hands, the ash of me and the descent of me, and they are old friends, and they are planning something quiet, and it does not include a bell, it does not include a hall of folded chairs, it does not include the word *yes* said twice in a bright room to someone who is not

—

I fold the invitation into a boat.

I set it on the puddle of everything I did not get to keep.

It sinks the way I knew it would. It goes down carrying my small white name into the drain, into the pipe that forgot, and I stand there in the powder of my own former heart

and I clap. Slowly. For you.

For the marriage. For the mouth that chose the other mouth.

The bees applaud with their wings and the dust applauds by coming down and I am so full of severed, love, I am so full of the clean cut and the quiet after,

that I could almost, from here, from this sinking, from this floor beneath the floor,

wish you well.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a prose poem about unrequited love and the pain of watching someone else's wedding, using disjointed syntax and invented words like "rememory" and "unplanning."
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Chapel Keeps

The bells rememory a version of us that never—white doves against a sky I keep unplanning back into ordinary Tuesday, the one where you turned and it was me, was always going to be.

Here in the fourth pew, the flowers gossip in a language of *almost.* Lilies. You told me once you hated lilies. I hold this fact like a coin in a country that no longer takes it.

The way she walks toward you: a slow undrowning. And I am fluent now in the grammar of hands, how yours find hers without the small hesitation, that stutter-catch you used to give the world before you touched it. I collected those hesitations. I thought they were mine.

Vows spill their sugared certainties and something in me *ungathers,* comes apart at seams I stitched in secret, in the dark, in the long unyearing of years I spent believing patience was a form of prophecy.

I rememory your laugh across a kitchen that was never ours. The imagined mornings. The children with your eyes I had already half-named. All of it foldable now, all of it origami I must unfold back into flat and ordinary paper.

Applause. The kiss. The whole room *yeses* and I mouth it too—

because love, the real kind, is a thing you learn to say into the wind and mean it, even as it carries nothing back, even as you stand here *becoming smaller,* practicing the ancient art of the almost-gone, the graceful un-being of the one who stayed too long inside a maybe.

The doors open. Light unrooms us all.

I go out into a weather that has no name for what I am.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an emotionally intense, stream-of-consciousness poem in second person, blending tenderness and despair, that ends with the loneliness of hearing hearts beating in separate rooms.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the House Knows at 3 A.M.**

You are the hand I memorized in the dark, the knuckles
I counted like rosary beads when the fever took me,
you are the voice that said *stay, stay, I've got you*
and I believed it, God, I believed it the way
a child believes the ceiling is the sky—

and now you turn, you turn away, the sheets
a country between us with its own weather,
its cold front moving in, and I want to say your name
but my mouth is full of all the things I never said,
the *thank you* and the *I'm sorry* and the *don't you dare
disappear inside yourself where I can't reach*—

remember the kitchen, the flour on your cheek,
how I kissed it off and you laughed like water finding
the crack in stone, how the light came sideways
through the blinds and striped us gold, remember
we were animals of the same warm den—

but something happened, didn't it, something
so quiet I couldn't name the moment it began,
a hairline, a held breath, a door left ajar
that neither of us walked through, and now
I lie here loving you so hard it hurts my teeth,
my whole body a fist around the wanting—

and you are down the hall, I know the sound
of your breathing changing into sleep,
I know it like my own pulse, and this is the cruelty,
this is the thing no one tells you:
you can lose someone who is still alive,
still here, still under the same roof—

and I lie awake and listen, and I swear
I can hear it, yours and mine,
two hearts beating in separate rooms.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
